utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Harmon, are you ready to continue the cross-examination of the witness, Mr. Stavnjak?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Usher, you're invited to escort Mr. Stavnjak into the courtroom. I use the time available at this moment. We started five minutes late, I do understand, for technical reasons. Now and then, both on the part of the Court and on the part of the parties, it happens that we have a late start, where it's not technical reasons, but late arrival, to say it this way. In view of the time restraints we have, the Chamber would very much like to improve its own and everyone else's discipline in this courtroom to start in due time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, that was not for you, as you will understand. Mr. Stavnjak, I'd like to remind you that you gave yesterday a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and that you're still - I would say it goes without saying - bound by that solemn declaration. Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stavnjak.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, yesterday you told us you went to Cajnice. In 2001 and 2002, you were Dusko Kornjaca's deputy, were you not?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what was the position of Mr. Kornjaca in 2001 and 2002?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period of time -- well, in the year 2000, after the local elections, which took place on the 6th of April, 2000, he was appointed as the mayor of the Municipality of Cajnice, and I was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday that you had served in the VRS up until the Dayton Peace Accords. What was the unit in which you served?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked in a unit which belonged to the Municipality of Cajnice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the number or designation of that unit?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. We used to call it the Cajnice Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understood your examination yesterday, your evidence, that you were an infantryman. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you participate in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you participate in combat operations against the enclave of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part, it was the demarcation line which was set up later on, after the withdrawal of the Serb population from the Municipality of Gorazde. So there was this demarcation line and that's where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the corps with which your unit was associated? Was it the Drina Corps or the Herzegovina Corps, or was it some other corps?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I can't remember exactly, but, well, I was there for three or three and a half years. And things changed on a number of occasions between the Herzegovina and Drina Corps. But I can't remember exactly. I think that most of the time we were within the Herzegovina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you participate in any military actions against the enclave of Zepa or the enclave of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn to a different topic, Mr. Stavnjak. Do you know a man by the name of Vojislav Krunic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krunic was a member of the SDS Executive Board in 1991 and 1992, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vojislav Krunic wasn't a member for as long as I was within the leadership, or for as long as I was working for the authorities of the Municipality of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps I framed the question improperly. Mr. Krunic was a member of the SDS Executive Board at the higher level, not at the municipal level, but at the level at the centre, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you have contacts with Mr. Krunic in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had contacts with Mr. Krunic in 1990 and up until the first half of 1991, for as long as I was within the leadership of the SDS party at Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krunic was a member of the SDS, was he not?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not quite correct, because I kept all the records and I don't recall him ever joining the party, ever signing the papers to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have presented evidence from Mr. Treanor indicating that Mr. Krunic was a member of the SDS Executive Board from 1991 to 1992. I can give Your Honours the citation on that. And we also have his attendance records at the SDS Executive Board. So I will provide that to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's talk about another individual, Mr. Stavnjak, Hadzo Efendic, the man who you described in your testimony yesterday as a tough cookie in his negotiations. Is this the same Mr. Efendic who was appointed the first vice-president or the deputy Prime Minister of the Bosnia-Herzegovina government in February of 1993?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he had that position, deputy prime minister, as you call it, because at that time I was involved in other issues and I was not engaged in politics in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you - you may not know the answer to this - but in October of 1993 Mr. Efendic was appointed the ambassador to Austria. Do you have any reason to dispute that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really am not familiar with this information. My children were at Miljen and the demarcation line between the Muslim forces and the Serb forces was very close and I was involved in these matters which helped me protect my own life and the lives of my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, again with leave of the Court, I can present official documents from the Gazette establishing those two appointments, and if the Court -- if it's disputed, otherwise, if counsel - - and I can talk about it during the recess and perhaps I can show those documents to counsel and he can enter into a stipulation if he's so inclined.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we certainly consider that the witness doesn't seem to have expressed a view one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness does not contradict it, but of course the mere fact that the witness doesn't know about something doesn't mean that it's therefore true. So I do understand Mr. Harmon would like to present to you documents to see whether you can make any stipulation as to Mr. Efendic being appointed as deputy prime minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. I was offering to be helpful. I was just suggesting really on points like this, I'm very open to Mr. Harmon putting them in front of me. But then they seem immediately, when a witness has got nothing to say, they seem immediately to have nothing to do with that witness, and outside Court no doubt we can consider such points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, let's turn to the topic that we discussed yesterday, and that was the post-multi-party election discussions between the SDS and the SDA for positions of power in the Municipality of Gorazde. First off, in those multi-party elections, the SDS won 13 of 50 seats in those elections; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, approximately, yes. I can't confirm whether it was exactly 13, but you might be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the SDA won 29 out of 50 seats. Do you have any reason to dispute that fact, Mr. Stavnjak?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that must be, more or less, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your evidence yesterday, Mr. Stavnjak - I'm referring to the transcript at page 71 - you concluded your evidence, direct examination, by saying the following. I'm starting at line 4: "This fits in, so to say, with what I said in the beginning of the afternoon, that is to say, that those talks with Mr. Efendic were very difficult and tiresome, and that there was no agreement in the end. So those people who followed in my and Mr. Begovic's footsteps in the SDS in Gorazde were unable to reach any agreement at all, and that's why this tragic conflict broke out. Of course, I would like to say that Mr. Efendic, or rather, the SDA in Gorazde, bears most responsibility for this tragic conflict, because the responsibility is always in the hands of those who have absolute power. And at that time, it was the SDA which had absolute power in Gorazde, so they had to show some tolerance, and I think they are really to blame to quite a considerable extent." You blame the SDA for the failure of the negotiations to divide power in the Municipality of Gorazde; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The fact is that the key reason why the SDA didn't give the SDS a single seat or a single position in the municipal power was because the SDS failed to join the Gorazde Municipal Assembly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. It is correct that Serb councilors did not participate in the first assembly precisely because no agreement had been reached previously in multi-party talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But the reason they didn't get any positions was because they didn't participate in the Municipal Assembly; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but when you set up the executive authority at the local level, everything needs to be put down on paper, the entire procedure, or at least a part of it, depending on how the parties agree. And then you have to sign it, and then you can go ahead and have the first assembly meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we distribute the next exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it need a number, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is a letter to President Karadzic, dated the 25th of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Registrar, that would have which number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be, Your Honours, P966.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, you have in front of you the Bosnian version of P966. This is, as I say, a letter to President Karadzic, president of the Serb Democratic Party. And if you turn to the last page in the B/C/S version, you'll see 14 signatures. If I can direct your attention, Mr. Stavnjak, to a line that says: "Lazar Stavnjak" and has a signature. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this is a document -- I want to read part of this document. You're familiar with it, Mr. Stavnjak, because you were one of the authors of this document. I want to read a portion of this document to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I'm referring, Your Honour, to the second paragraph on page 2 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Second sentence I start. It says: "Our failure to join the Assembly is the key reason why to this day the SDA has not given us a single position in municipal power. Dr. Mojovic and a group of like-minded people are the sole culprits for our boardsmen failing to enter the Assembly and for failing to reach an agreement with the SDA." The reason why you didn't achieve positions in the government was because you weren't cooperating in the Municipal Assembly; isn't that correct, Mr. Stavnjak?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the key phrase is the one that you've just read out, that is to say, the basic problem was that Mr. Efendic wanted us to attend the first assembly. That was the whole point. And talks were meant to take place afterwards, on the power-sharing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever join the Municipal Assembly of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very soon after this date, the date of this document, I left the actual leadership of the SDS in Gorazde, and Mr. Begovic and Mr. Kosoricas as well. New people came along and they were involved in these talks, and what happened afterwards, I think we all know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the Serbs ever join the Gorazde Municipal Assembly, either before you left or after you left?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the SDS never joined the work of the Assembly in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to the second paragraph, and I want to ask you a question about a portion of that paragraph. I'm referring to the second -- I'm going to start in the second sentence of that document, second paragraph. Actually, I'll start at the beginning. "As you are probably already familiar with the situation inside the Municipal Board in Gorazde, we would try to describe the chronological order that what led to such a situation, because we feel that we need to inspect the causes that led to such a situation rather than deal with its consequences. In our opinion, it started with the meeting and consultation held in Koran about the distribution of power in the municipalities." Now, what was the problem at Koran that you're referring to in this letter?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the basic issue. Some members of the party considered that it was necessary for us to get a certain amount of power, and people Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. had different opinions as to what positions they should get. People's views differ, but we had to reach some kind of agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So while there may have been some disagreements, can you explain to me what the problems were at Koran, what were the differences of opinion, then, that are referred to emanating from the meeting that was held at the Koran?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that was the key issue, in fact. Some people considered that it would be a good idea to attend the Assembly without any agreement, whereas others tended to think that we had to reach some kind of agreement beforehand in order to give a kind of legitimacy to the Assembly. And if we attended the Assembly, by virtue of that very fact, we would be giving it legitimacy. So that was the disagreement. Do we give this legitimacy to the Assembly without any agreement or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Which camp did you fall into, Mr. Stavnjak?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can't really talk about camps, just differences of opinion within the executive -- or rather, the municipal committee. But I think my actions afterwards showed that I was rather wise in what I did. More- educated people, I'm not going to say whether they were more intelligent or not, but more-educated people followed me in my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Which position did you adopt? Were you in favour of joining the municipality without an agreement or were you in favour of not joining the municipality until there was an agreement on power?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had my own opinion. I thought that it would be better to attend the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me turn to the next sentence following the one I just read, and I want to ask your comments on this: "Stanoje Begovic, the President of the Gorazde Municipal Board, and Lazar Stavnjak, the Secretary of the Municipal Board, were said to be present at the meeting. In the absence of the president and the secretary, Dr. Mladen Mojovic, the vice-president of the Municipal Board, selected and held a meeting of the Municipal Board on 8 December 1990, at which he criticised distinguished Serb," and then it's illegible, "and determined three additional negotiators with the SDA, Dusko Tos, Slobodan Gojkovic, and Blazo Ignjatovic, even though up to that point it was Begovic, Mojovic, and Stankovic [sic] who were supposed to negotiate with the SDA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it you were to say Stavnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Stavnjak, if I miss pronounced that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you comment on that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That negotiating team was extended afterwards with the addition of the last three names that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There was considerable dissent within the SDS, was there not? Didn't it eventually result in a coup within the SDS?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, certainly not. There were just differences of opinion, and that was normal for those times. I mean, we were not used to a multi- party system, so we were beginners, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, on page 2, it's 2 of the English, Your Honour. It's the fourth paragraph down, there's a portion of this letter that reads as follows: "It was around that time that the aforementioned group started with the first false accusations of certain members of the Municipal Board, claiming they were spies, Milos Carapic, Ranko Andric. These false accusations spread to Stanko Stojanovic, Ostas Kosoric and the secretary, Lazar Stavnjak. After this, they started calling and holding municipal meetings without the knowledge of the party president and secretary. This meant that a coup had been struck in the Municipal Board of the SDS in Gorazde." Now, these are your words to President Karadzic. So I asked you earlier, Mr. Stavnjak, wasn't there a coup within the SDS? And your answer was "no." So let me repeat the question. Wasn't there a coup in the SDS?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Certainly you can call it that. We dealt with it through our agreement. If the president of the Municipal Board and the secretary of the Municipal Board withdrew voluntarily and they were replaced by other people, then you can't call this a coup.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why did you call it a coup to President Karadzic, then?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I cannot say whether there is a word of that sort in the text, a coup. I'm familiar with this document, but I don't see the word "coup" anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As soon as there's an interpretation issue, which seems to be the case, I'd like to have it clarified through our interpreters. May I ask the attention of the interpreters, the second page of the B/C/S version, which -- the paragraph which seems to start with the words "u to vreme" that paragraph. Whether at the end of that paragraph, the last sentence, which is translated into English "this meant that a coup had been struck in the Municipal Board of the SDS in Gorazde," whether, especially in view of the translation "coup," whether there would be any comment from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If you can just give us a minute. We're waiting for the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You hadn't received it. Yes, then I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the B/C/S booth has found this portion of the text, and indeed the word is putsch, or coup, literal translation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last word on the semi-last line in that paragraph, where it reads "putsch," is that the word we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say, far be it for us to disagree, but we do agree. Mr. Sladojevic, the Defence acknowledges that that word is aptly translated in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Stavnjak, now everyone seems to agree, Prosecution, Defence, interpreters, that the word used in the text is "putsch," which seems to be the word as we know it in the German language as well, which stands for a coup. Does this change your mind that such a word is used in this letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't agree with that. It all depends on the translation. I still have not found the word "putsch" in this text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Third paragraph, starting with "u to vreme" at the semi-last line, I apologise for my pronunciation. That's where the word "putsch" seems to appear. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, but the letter C here is almost illegible. That's why I wouldn't find the word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You found it now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you agree that means coup or "putsch"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what you can see in the document, but if you read on, you will see that we held another session of the Municipal Board and that we agreed on how to deal with the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand your explanation. But it's now clearly established that there's no interpretation issue involved. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just say, because Your Honour knows I'm trying to do my best. I stood up expressly to say that I agreed and it's appearing in the transcript that I disagreed, and I hope Your Honour would know that I'm just sensitive to make sure that such errors don't creep in. That's page 11, line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think Your Honour understands I'd like such things to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Stavnjak, we're still focusing on -- I now want to focus on the negotiations that took place with Mr. Efendic. In fact, when you say he was a tough negotiator, there were six negotiators from the SDS and only three from the SDA during those negotiations; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later on, the number was expanded to six.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn to a different document. We'll distribute this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just try to understand your testimony. Was the issue that it if it would come to voting, that you were afraid that all Serbs would be outvoted in the Assembly meeting and that, therefore, you thought it better to have an agreement, or at least you tried to have an agreement before it came to any voting? And is that what you're talking about in this letter later on, where you are -- where it says "non- democratic elections and the result of that"? Is that a proper understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you referring to the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the Municipal Assembly, we could not -- there were 29 out of 50 members of the Assembly from the SDA. They had an absolute majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were afraid that without an agreement you'd go to that Assembly, that you'd get nothing at all, because on every vote there would be a majority of Serbs; is that a correct understanding of the problem you had at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. That is correct. I believe that Your Honour has just said the key word. If we had joined the Assembly and if we had made it legal, we would still not have received anything in the system of power-sharing in the town, and that is the essence of the whole problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, let me show you the next exhibit. Mr. Stavnjak, you're getting another exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is an exhibit, Your Honour, that has previously been exhibited. It's P43 and P64A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's especially this one that got those numbers, because we know that there are many of them. Yes, I see that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm informed it is, Your Honour. This particular copy has copy number 93 on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to review that document, Mr. Stavnjak?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This document, for the record, Your Honour, is essentially instructions for the organisation and operation of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in emergency conditions. This is a document that we referred to as Variant A and Variant B.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you could turn, please, Mr. Stavnjak, to the last page of the Bosnian version that is in front of you, the top line, in handwriting. It's in handwriting, Mr. Stavnjak. You should have that. Turn to the last page, in handwriting, Mr. Stavnjak. In handwriting, at the top, it says: "93A." It says "Stojan" and "Gorazde." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Did you attend the meeting in Sarajevo on the 19th of December, 1991, where these instructions were issued?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. At that time, I was already the secretary of the Serbian Cultural Society that had been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who at your municipality did attend the meeting in Sarajevo on the 19th of December, the Main Board meeting? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This document, I just want to take you through this very quickly, Mr. Stavnjak, because I'm going to be asking you some questions in a minute. This document was created and distributed for the purpose of implementing a decision for the Serbian people to live in one state, and it makes a distinction between municipalities where Serbs formed a majority of the population and where they formed a minority of the population. And it outlines certain steps that needed to be taken in order to create parallel institutions in the municipality. Now, you've never heard of this document; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me show you another exhibit, then, Mr. Stavnjak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it need a number, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not quite sure whether we're on the same topic. May I simply observe when Mr. Harmon said at line 14 of the previous page, he asked: "Did you attend the meeting in Sarajevo on the19th of December, 1991, where those instructions were issued?" That not being put to the witness or the second element, we know that is the Prosecution's case, but that contains an assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would agree with you that there seems to be a dispute between the parties, but I took it from the answer of the witness that he did not attend that meeting at all. So what supposedly has happened during that meeting seems then not very relevant for the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not making a major issue of it. If we were going to be continuing with this topic, I felt it best simply to mention that minor point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. You may proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there a number on this? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's where we were. It is number -- yes. The reason I hesitated is that it is a handwritten document, original ERN number 00596545, starting with "1A establish around the clock", we'll get a better description, and at the very end, rosters, at least one roster. Mr. Harmon, if you could give us in three words, but perhaps first ask the witness what this document is, because it's not easy to describe it on the basis of what we have in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. These are handwritten notes, Your Honour, that relate to the previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Handwritten note, and you just add the ERN number of the original --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P967, Your Honours. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, these are handwritten notes. You have them in front of you. Do you recognise the handwriting on these notes?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've never seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to the first handwritten item, which, according to the English translation, says: "1. Establish around the clock shifts in all SDS Municipal Boards. B. Secure." If we compare that to Variant B, the previous document, on page 7 of the English translation, one will see the words "introduce around the clock duty service in all SDS Municipal Boards and ensure constant communication and cooperation with all local boards on the territory of the municipality." Mr. Stavnjak, you left the municipality in April of 1992, as I understood your evidence yesterday. Did the SDS introduce around the clock duty service in all SDS duty boards while you were still in the Municipality of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were in the Gorazde municipality, you left in April of 1992, did the SDS establish around-the-clock duty service in the SDS Municipal Boards?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know, because I did not participate in the work of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn to the second item of this handwritten note. It says: "Sessions of SEC -- of SDS Municipal Board every day at 1700 hours."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I've got SDS instead of SEC -- oh, you corrected it yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I direct Your Honours' attention to Variant B, number 2, which says: "Ensure conditions for daily meetings of the SDS Municipal Board secretariat to allow constant monitoring and assessment of the situation on the ground and the taking of necessary measures."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Stavnjak: Did the SDS Municipal Board, after the 19th of December, 1991, have meetings every day?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know, and I can't answer your question. You have to understand that I was not a member of the inner leadership. I did not attend the meetings. I was a member of the cultural society. That's what I've already stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, may I just ask you one question before we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You present P967.1 as one document, and from your questioning, you seem to relate that to the 19th of December, 1991 instructions. At the same time, the roster, at the very end, seems to concentrate on October 1991. So that would even be before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: These aren't necessarily in order, Your Honour, these documents. When these documents were collected, I'm not sure what order they were put in, but they were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, I'm asking you. You say you present them as one document, and therefore, I think you well understood my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I did understand your question, and I'm going to be referring to certain parts of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, tying in with Your Honour's observation, it might be appropriate if Mr. Harmon were to make it clearer to the witness exactly what he says this document this is. Because the witness said he'd never seen it and it hasn't really been indicated to him what the Prosecution suggests it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I suggested, Your Honour, these are handwritten documents. I can tell Your Honours these were documents that were seized in Gorazde and provided to us by the authorities -- by the Bosnian government authorities. And that's why I'd like to go through this document with this witness, and perhaps he can illuminate what's in it for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not -- that's not really quite good enough, with respect. If the Prosecution are going to -- if they're going to use this document in the cross-examination to the witness, they ought to go as far as they can in making it clear what they say. The various bits - and Your Honour quite correctly points out, it's apparently not a single document - what they say the bits of the document actually are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's clear from the examination the bits of the document relate to Variant A and Variant B, and that's what we're asserting and putting to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand -- let me try and cut this short. Do I understand, Mr. Harmon, that the Prosecution considers this to be handwritten notes which it considers to be created as a result of the 19th of December instructions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Not knowing, perhaps yet, who drafted it, perhaps you do know, but until now we haven't heard anything about that. Then, Mr. Stewart, where I first pointed at a roster which seems to relate to October 1991, I also see in the handwritten notes, which seem to be in a different handwriting, or at least not in the same -- not -- yes, seems to be in a different handwriting, that it refers to a first meeting to be held on the 26th of December, 1991. Therefore, it seems that these documents might not really belong together. At least, I note at this moment that two different time frames seem to be reflected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. That's correct. And I will get to that, Your Honour. I will address that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you said that you were in the cultural society. My question, then, is: Did you hear about daily meetings of the SDS Municipal Board, even though you weren't a member? Did you hear about daily members of the SDS Municipal Board while you remained in the Municipality of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's turn to number 3 of this handwritten document. It says: "Crisis Staff." And it has a list of names, starting with Milosova Herin, President Dusko Tosic, and it goes down through, it appears to be, the name of Slavica Gavrilovic [phoen]. Now, are you aware that the SDS did create a Crisis Staff in the Municipality of Gorazde in late 1991 and early 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you recognise the names that are on this list in front of you as being people who were members of the SDS in the Municipality of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know most of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know if any of these people were in positions of responsibility and leadership within the municipal SDS party?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Herin was President of the Municipal Board. Mr. Bosko Sekaric [phoen] was in my position. He replaced me in the position of the Secretary of the Municipal Board. Mladen Mojovic was Vice-President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. We can't go beyond that evidence that you have -- you weren't aware of any crisis staff in the municipality. Let me turn to the fourth item in this handwritten note, and the fourth item says: "Call and proclaim the Assembly of the Serbian People." That's sub-part A. And sub-part B says: "The Assembly consists of members of Serbian nationality at the Assembly and presidents of the Municipal Boards." And then it lists Slavomir Gavrilovic, coordinator of the SDA, it says, and others. And then it lists board members and it lists 29 people. Now, who are those people?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have not seen this document before. Your Honours, if you will allow me to say that this text does not bear any stamp, and it is in the Latin script. And I know that as from the 1990, when I was a member of the local leadership in Gorazde, we used the Cyrillic script, and we always wrote in the Cyrillic. I've seen some of the documents that they were done in the Cyrillic, and as for this document, which is in the Latin script, I really don't know what to say. I couldn't comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are the people who are listed, Mr. Stavnjak, from 1 to 29, were those members of the Serbian Assembly?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them are members of the Assembly, because the SDS had 13 members, as you have said it yourself. And I believe that all of their names are here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I invite Your Honours to compare this item number 4 with item number 4 in the Variant A and Variant B document that we provided previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when was the first Assembly, Serbian Assembly, convened, Mr. Stavnjak? Was it convened on December 26th, 1991?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You were still a member of the SDS in December of 1991, or were you in the cultural association?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the SDS throughout all that time. I'm still a member, for that matter. And the Serbian Cultural Society was established towards the end of 1991. I can't give you the exact date, but I'm sure that I was not a member of the Municipal Board. I was a member of the SDS. I was then, and I still am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention to item number 8. There is a list of four people in item number 8. One of them is Mr. Arsic. Do you see that name in front of you, Arsic? Who is Mr. Arsic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, this is in the Latin script. I know Mr. Arsic personally. If that's the man we're referring to, because I can only see his family name here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was Mr. Arsic the commander of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says Arsic here, but there's no first name. I used to know --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there a man named Arsic who was involved with the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We'll come back to that. Number 9 on this document, Mr. Stavnjak, it says: "Inform the Serbian people not to travel," and then it has the initials "GO." Now, was there ever --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I turn Your Honours' attention to number 9 in the previous document, that reads "advise the Serbian staff they must not go on annual leave, travel abroad or leave their permanent residence in the coming period."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, were you aware that, at any point in time while you were in the Municipality of Gorazde, that the Serbian staff was advised not to go on annual leave, not to travel, not to go abroad, not to leave their place of residence?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So it is your testimony, finally, that you can't assist us with this document, you can't assist us with when the Serb Assembly convened?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know when it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, in late 1991 and early 1992, before the conflict broke out in Gorazde, were the Serbs arming themselves?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were the Serbs getting arms from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, just for my information, you told the Chamber that these documents were seized in Gorazde and provided by the Bosnian government authorities. Would you have any more detail about where in Gorazde they were found?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will make that inquiry, Your Honour. I can tell Your Honours as well where the other document was seized, the previous document, if Your Honours are interested, Variant A and Variant B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The Variant A and Variant B document, Your Honour, was seized in the Holiday Inn, in the Boksit office, and it was provided to us along with other documents that were seized from the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Holiday Inn in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sarajevo, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, do these documents need an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They do not, Your Honour. I can tell you, the first --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They do not, Your Honour. The first document that I'm going to be referring to is an analysis of combat readiness and activities of the Army of Republika Srpska in 1992. It's previously been exhibited as P64A, P529, binder 6, tab 255. And I have taken excerpts out of this. I'd like to present this to -- certain quotes to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, this first document that you have in front of you is a document that is a document that was prepared by the army of the Republika Srpska. It is a military secret and it was prepared in April of 1993, and it reflects back on the status of the army in 1992. And I want to read a portion of this document to you and ask you some questions about it. Under -- on page 14 -- actually, starting at page 13, there's a reference to units of the infantry. On page 14 of the English, second paragraph, this says, and I quote: "The infantry units formed are equipped with weapons received from the former JNA which were distributed by officers, members of the Serbian Democratic Party, or other representatives of the Serbian people." Can you comment on that, Mr. Stavnjak? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, have you found it, Mr. Stavnjak? Have you found the portion just read? You find it at the page 13, at the bottom, going -- no. It starts even on the top of page 14.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll repeat what I read, Mr. Stavnjak, to assist you: "The infantry units formed are equipped with weapons received from the former JNA which were distributed by officers, members of the Serbian Democratic Party, or other representatives of the Serbian people." Do you know about that, Mr. Stavnjak?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this document before, so I'm really unable to comment on it. I've only just set eyes on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to comment on the document. I'm asking you to comment on the events described in the document. And the events described in the document are that the SDS was helping to distribute weapons to representatives of the Serbian people. Do you know anything about that, Mr. Stavnjak?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me quote to you another passage, Mr. Stavnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This, Your Honour, is a quotation from General Gvero, and it is from the 34th Assembly Session of the Assembly that was held on the 29th of September, 1993. The quotation I'm going to be referring to is found in exhibit P64A, P65, Treanor, binder 16, tab 221.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And let me quote General Gvero, Mr. Stavnjak: "The Serb Democratic Party has politically aroused and united the Serb nation. It has formulated their political and social goals and organised all the preconditions for the success of fighting." Then I'm going to drop down to the first paragraph that follows that portion. It's on page 354 in the English, Your Honours: "The SDS and the state institutions that have been established take the most credits for arming the Serb people with personal weapons, which was made possible by the support of many Serb officers and the commands of the former JNA on the territory of the former BiH. Serbs working in the internal affairs institutions and in the political institutions of the army Serbia, and SJR also contributed to this. In May 1992, after the JNA left our territory, the army of the Republika Srpska was established," and it goes on. Now, Mr. Stavnjak, again, this is General Gvero talking about the SDS taking the most credits for arming the Serbian people with personal weapons. Do you have any -- does that refresh your recollection or does that assist you in recalling the events that took place in Gorazde or in areas around Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've just scanned this document, the bit that you've just read out, and my only comment, if I may, is that the SDS led to a political awakening of the Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that's what it says in the first sentence, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to distribute one more document, Your Honour. This is a document that is P51, previously exhibited. This document, Your Honour, has, first of all, a cover letter from General Kukanjac to the JNA General Staff. What this document is is the conclusions of the evaluation of the situation of the BiH territory -- on the BiH territory in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Military District. It is a military secret. It has been exhibited as P51 in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, I want to refer you to a portion of this document. In the B/C/S version, it is found on page 4. If you turn to -- page 5. I'm sorry. Page 5 of the document. Do you have page 5 in front of you, Mr. Stavnjak?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I have no -- I have a page 4, and the next one has been handwritten 172, but the 5 does not appear. But it seems there's double numbering on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was referring to the B/C/S version, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was looking at the B/C/S version, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm referring, then, to the ERN number at the top, then, that has -- ends in digit 7209.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I wonder whether we have the same document in front of us, because I have -- last four digits always 0, and then ranging from 106 until 116. So there might be a problem. I'm talking about the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Apparently there are two different copies with two different sets of numbers. I will refer to the set of numbers that Your Honours have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we then perhaps have a copy shown to the witness on the ELMO? Or perhaps refer to the original P51 and have that on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can direct the witness, Your Honour, to the right page, then. I'm sorry for the delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, the document you have in front of you has at the top, it has numbers that read -- it's on page 4 of the document, and on the top you'll see number 02100109. That's the page where the portion I'm interested in starts. And I am particularly interested on the next page, the next page, sub-part E. And in the English version of this document, Your Honours, I'm interested in directing Your Honours' attention to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems to be in the paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Page 6, and it is sub-part E on page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you see the portion I'm referring to, Mr. Stavnjak?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this confidential report from General Kukanjac, do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him myself, but I heard he was a general who, at the time, was -- I don't know whether he was a commander of the 6th Sarajevo District in the former JNA, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And this portion that I've referred you to, Mr. Stavnjak, it deals with volunteer units in the zone of the 2nd Military District. And under sub-part E, it reads as follows: "On the territory of the 4th Military District, in the municipalities Kalinovik, Foca, Cajnice, Gorazde, there are 6.500 people in volunteer units (that was formed earlier by the 4th Corps)." This document is dated March 20th, 1992. What can you tell us about those volunteer units, Mr. Stavnjak, that were formed in the Municipality of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about the formation of these units at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to dispute General Kukanjac in his confidential report, that such units were formed in your district?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first I've heard of it. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you don't dispute General Kukanjac when he asserts this in a confidential military secret document that went to the headquarters, to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer the question, because I'm not familiar with these matters at all, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: One final question on the issue of arming, Mr. Stavnjak. What can you tell the Trial Chamber about the delivery of 30 tonnes of weapons and ammunition that were shipped from it Pale to the village of Odzak and later distributed to the Serbs? Can you tell us anything about that event?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn, then, my attention to another topic, Mr. Stavnjak. We're finished with that document. Thank you. Did the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're going to distribute another document, Mr. Stavnjak. This next document, Your Honour, is a document that's been previously exhibited. It's P64A and P65, Treanor, 11, tab 113. It is from the 12th Session of the Assembly of the Bosnian Serb People, held in Pale on the 24th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention, Mr. Stavnjak --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, I want to direct your attention to a decision on the verification of decisions on the proclamation of newly established Serbian municipalities passed by municipal assemblies. And this verification of a decision lists municipalities passed by municipal assemblies, and it lists the newly-established Serbian municipalities in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and verifies them. And one of the locations where this is verified is in Gorazde. What can you tell us about that, Mr. Stavnjak? Do you know anything about the proclamation of Serbian assemblies that were established in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a problem, but ... If you don't speak through the microphone, Mr. Krajisnik, it will not be ... Yes, it's internal communication, I do understand, between Mr. Krajisnik and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps this discussion could take place during the recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends on whether it's relevant for what happens at this moment in Court, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik is having difficulty I think finding the spot in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I could -- if I -- let's have a look at it. I see that it's under decision. Mr. Krajisnik, it says [B/C/S spoken] under 8, and then we come to a decision, and on the top of page 41, the last municipality mentioned in the B/C/S copy is Gorazde. Yes? You found it? Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I wanted to clarify -- Mr. Stavnjak, I wanted to clarify part of your testimony yesterday. You were discussing the theft of explosives from the factory at Pobjeda, at page 25 of your testimony. I just want a brief clarification. You testified as follows. This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm referring, Your Honour, to lines 23 through 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You were discussing hearing about explosives and explosive devices being taken out of the factory, and you said, at line 24: "It was mostly employees of Muslim nationality, in fact, that were involved." Were members of other nationalities also taking out explosives?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, because they were not in a position to do so, because of the kind of management we had and because of the physical conditions and security service there. So there were guards, et cetera. And it wasn't possible to enter the premises without an adequate pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So what did you mean by the word "mostly employees of Muslim nationality," in your evidence yesterday?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have said that but, of course, if one nationality controls the comings and goings with regard to any given company, the other nationality would not have been in a position to engage in any such activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't care to belabour the point, Mr. Stavnjak. Let's talk about the rising tensions that took place in your municipality, about which you testified yesterday. You testified about an incident at a petrol station on the 11th of March, and you said that that was the first incident relating to inter-ethnic tensions. And you said that: "Serbs set up barricades where they made up a majority." And you used the word "barricades." I'm referring to page 33, lines 22 to 23. And later in your evidence, Mr. Stavnjak, you said: "The Serbs set up just one checkpoint." Now, what was it, Mr. Stavnjak? Did they set up, after this incident at the petrol station, did they set up one barricade or did they set up more than one barricade?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, because I was in my flat - I couldn't see it all - but on the basis of what I heard, there was a checkpoint towards our church.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So is it -- you don't know whether they set up one or more than one barricade; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I heard there was a single barricade in front of the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This, Your Honour, is a media report from Tanjug. It's dated the 21st of March - I'm sorry - yes, dated the 21st of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it not yet in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's not in evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P968, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, this is in English, so let me read this to you. This is a report from Tanjug. It's dated the 21st of March, 1992, and it says: "The National Defence Council of the Gorazde Municipal Assembly, in which there are no representatives of the Serbian nation, proclaimed a state of emergency today and adopted a decision restricting the movement of all people other than those working for those services needed to maintain life as usual. Special territorial defence units have also been mobilised. The state of emergency was proclaimed after Serbs, dissatisfied with several months of gasoline rationing, erected barricades near gasoline stations last night. Mayor Hadzo Efendic, who was also chairman of the party of the Democratic Action's municipal committee, refused to talk with representatives of the Herzegovina assembly delegation, and republican Internal Affairs Ministry representatives are expected in Gorazde. Meanwhile, barricades have been erected by both the Serbs and the Muslims." So, Mr. Stavnjak, this article suggests there's more than one barricade in Gorazde set up by the Serbs, also suggests there's more than Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. one barricade set up by the Muslims. Do you have any reason to disagree with this Tanjug report?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, there was just one barricade in an inhabited area called Rijeka, and it's near the church, as far as the Serb barricades were concerned. And, of course, there were quite a few more on the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see that barricade?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just heard of it from my relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were the Serbs armed at that barricade?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's what my relatives told me. And I told you what I saw when I went to the shops.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to ask you about another incident, Mr. Stavnjak. Perhaps you can assist us with this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the copy we received, it seems to be the result of some highlighting which makes parts illegible. Is there any solution to that? And it seems to be in the next one as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can explain that. I prefer explaining that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- a little later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear, then, from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, this is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This needs an exhibit number as well, and this is a Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- network report.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P969, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll read this, Mr. Stavnjak, and maybe you can assist us with this, because this is dated the 23rd of March, 1992. It reads: "Sarajevo Radio Sarajevo network, and then --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, those who are listening to the French channel ask for my attention to your speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll slow down, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll read from the fourth line down. This is dated the 23rd of March, 1992: "As we have been informed by the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Trovrh radio transmitter was taken over yesterday afternoon. This transmitter was designated as a facility of a special importance for the republic by decree of the Executive Council of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The station was first surrounded and then taken over by a group of some 100 armed civilians of Serbian nationality. During this action, three employees of Sarajevo Radio and Television and two active militiamen of Serbian nationality from the Gorazde Police Station were inside the building." Mr. Stavnjak, what can you tell us about the takeover? First of all, can you tell us where the Trovrh radio transmitter is located? Is that in Gorazde municipality?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This TV transmitter is in the area of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this article -- this report reports 100 armed civilians of Serbian nationality. Can you comment on that, Mr. Stavnjak?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember this incident?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it on TV, when the reserve Serbian police went up to the Trovrh transmitter. I saw it on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What can you tell us about the policemen who were from Gorazde participating in this event?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I can't tell you anything about that. I don't know any of these facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This event, Mr. Stavnjak, coming approximately 12 days after the incident at the gas station, did this increase tensions within your community?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During that period of time, the inter-ethnic relations were rather tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did this increase the anxiety of the Muslim community within Gorazde municipality?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that. The only people that felt any anxiety were the Serbs, who were a minority in Gorazde, and they were the ones who were threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And why was it, in your opinion, Mr. Stavnjak, that the Muslims didn't feel any anxiety over the capture of a transmitter station that was used and had been used up to the time of its seizure for the transmission of radio emissions from Sarajevo? Let me phrase the question -- let me rephrase that again, Mr. Stavnjak. Once the radio transmitter was captured, are you aware that the transmitter was then directed so it could receive transmissions from Belgrade and not from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I'm looking at the clock. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: An hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's far beyond the 60 per cent, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will try to expedite it, Your Honour. I'll go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be aware that these rules, although not always strictly applied -- it's not a rule. Mr. Stewart would immediately correct me and say that it was a 60 per cent guidance only, but nevertheless, would you think over during the next break what is really essential. I mean, the Chamber has now heard during the examination-in- chief about quite a couple of incidents, and the Chamber has heard in the cross-examination about some other incidents, or read about some incidents, not heard very much about these incidents. Perhaps you could consider to what extent filling a basket with further incidents would assist the Chamber and look at what is really essential for your cross-examination. The Chamber might have some questions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I comment? I certainly wouldn't for one moment suggest that what we submit as a guideline for the Defence is a rule for the Prosecution. That wouldn't be fair. But Your Honour, it's this: It is very disruptive when we have no advance notification that the cross-examination is going to take longer. Some adjustment today has already been made. The result of this is further adjustment affecting people outside the courtroom, including the next witness, also then have to be made when the examination takes considerably longer. We're all flexible, Your Honour, but the more advance notice we have that it's going to take longer, the less disruption for all concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Judges will consider the matter during the break. But, Mr. Harmon, it might be a good idea that you at least put your list of witnesses such in order that the most important questions, that the most important questions are on top and prioritised already. We'll consider the matter and we will adjourn until 25 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the Chamber has considered the matter and expects you to -- those questions to the witness you could put to him in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: 15 minutes, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: 15 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, have you heard of the order by Mr. Mandic to separate the Serbian police from the Muslim police? Were you aware that that order was transmitted in late March?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the police in Gorazde separate?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did that create -- did that increase ethnic tensions in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they were tense already in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In addition to the events we've described that created or contributed to ethnic tension, were you aware of the events of the ethnic cleansing that had happened in Bijeljina with Arkan that occurred at the end of March of 1992? Had you heard about those events?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it on the media, but I can't claim for a fact that it was on that date or during that period of time. I heard it on TV and on radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You heard also that the city of Zvornik had been attacked by Arkan and that the city of Bratunac had been taken over by volunteers who had come in from Serbia? Were you aware of those events as well?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the events in Bijeljina contribute to the anxiety of the Muslim population in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Gorazde municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Gorazde municipality, the situation became tense in March, after the arrival of the Muslim extremists by Visegrad, headed by Volica Banovic, who publicly walked through the streets of Gorazde and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, I have 15 minutes. Did the events in Bijeljina, Foca, Zvornik and in Bratunac contribute to the Muslim population becoming anxious?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You described bridges being blockaded. How far was the Drina River in the location of those bridges from Serbia? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what bridges you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You described yesterday in your testimony three bridges that were blockaded in mid-April of 1992. How far were those bridges from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about the three bridges in the town of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct. I'm asking you how far away those bridges were - - you know, what was the distance between the Drina River at that location where the bridges were and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 50 kilometres or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn to your testimony yesterday, your evidence dealing with the Serbs that had left -- the exodus of Serbs that left Gorazde on the 26th and 27th of August, the Serbs that inhabited the left bank. And in your evidence, you said that the Serbs left in the direction of Rogatica, and that that exodus was not organised. I want to ask you some questions about that exodus. Isn't it a fact that on August 27th, Gorazde, which had been under a long siege, was now being relieved of the siege; the siege was being lifted? Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact, Mr. Stavnjak, that the Serb civilians were ordered by Serb soldiers to evacuate?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact, Mr. Stavnjak, that there was an organised convoy for the people who were leaving Gorazde in late August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the left bank?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the population that was not armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to show you an exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to read to you very briefly from an exhibit. I'm going to be quick with this exhibit, Mr. Stavnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is an exhibit that needs an exhibit number. It is an article from the New York Times dated the 16th of September, and it deals with the evacuation of Serbs on the 27th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P970, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This article, I just direct Your Honours' attention to the portion --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll read this to you, Mr. Stavnjak. It says: "The attack which the Serbs all say happened in the early afternoon of August 27th came at the beginning of the lifting of a long Serbian siege of Gorazde," and it goes on to say: "Serbian forces had effectively encircled Gorazde, and the conditions of the town had been extremely bad." This article deals with the attack on the convoy that you described in your evidence, and in the article it goes on to say: "Serbs interviewed in a hospital in Sokolac this week said that several hundred Serbian residents of the village of Jabuka and rural areas of Gorazde, north of Gorazde, were ordered by the retreating Serbian soldiers to form a convoy and leave." It quotes a woman by the name of Veljko Lasica [phoen] who says: "It was just afternoon of the 27th and we got instructions that women and children and older people had to evacuate." And then there was a convoy assembled. So this article -- do you have any reason to dispute that article, Mr. Stavnjak?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in English, and as far as I could follow your words, I agree that women, children, and the elderly were at a risk, and that the convoy left because their lives were at a risk. And they had to seek safer places, and one of them was towards Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not the question. The question was, where you testified yesterday that it was an uncoordinated leaving of the area, that Mr. Harmon puts it to you that those who left the area - I'm not saying whether there were good reasons to leave the area; that's a totally different matter - but they were instructed to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
