utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I believe that we understand each other. When I said yesterday that there was no organisation, what I meant was there was a tragedy. In any case, I don't know what happened. I don't know whether somebody issued an order to them or not. But as long as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there was a convoy, and as long as there was a tragedy that struck at one place, of course there was a lack of organisation. It goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, you also gave evidence yesterday about the Serbs leaving on the 18th and 19th of September from the right bank, and then you said that they left in the direction of Cajnice, and that Gorazde became ethnically clean. That was your evidence at page 54 of the transcript. The reason the Serbs left the right bank was because Muslim forces were advancing, not because they were ethnically cleansed, or ethnically cleansing the right bank of the Drina River; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is now a contradiction to what you formerly said, that Muslims in Gorazde were threatened. The ratio of forces in Gorazde was such that Serbs could not survive there. What I'm claiming here, as I said here, is that in Gorazde, it was the Serbs that were threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Stavnjak, was that the reason the Serbs from the right bank of the Drina River left was because they fled in the face of advancing Muslim forces; isn't that the case? They weren't ethnically cleansed by the Muslims; they fled in advance of a Muslim military advance.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to introduce the next exhibit. This is merely confirmatory to what the witness says. It's an ECMM report dated the 23rd of September, 1992. If I could have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P971, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I direct Your Honours to sub-part B of the exhibit, dealing with the reasons why Serbs left the municipality. Next I would like to turn my attention to some of your evidence yesterday, Mr. Stavnjak, at page 49 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said, and I quote: "In the first days of the war, all those inhabited areas, villages, houses inhabited by members of the Serb people were rounded up and they were taken to smaller collection centres." Do I understand this piece of your evidence to say that all of the Muslim -- all of the Serbian people in the municipality of Gorazde, once the war started on May 4th, were rounded up, arrested, and taken to collection centres? Did you mean that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't say all the people. Not all the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm not going to belabour that point, Mr. Stavnjak. You testified briefly about a detention centre in Vitkovici. Can you tell us how long that detention centre lasted? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I said that I had heard that from two people from the Carapic family, Momir and Milivoj Carapic, who had passed through some of these camps, and I got information from them. They were in the territory under the control of the Muslim units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you aware of a United Nations protection force unit being stationed in the village of Vitkovici in early 1994? Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I knew that in 1994 representatives of the international forces entered the area, but I didn't know where they were posted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to -- with my limited time, I will submit for the Court's examination an UNPROFOR civil police report dated May 19th, 1994. I'd like to reserve --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a contextual exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's a contextual exhibit, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then the next exhibit I'd like to turn our attention to in the remaining few minutes that I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, yesterday in your evidence you described a Orthodox church that had been destroyed in Gorazde. And in respect of the mosques that were in Gorazde, your testimony, at page 57, was: "Not a single mosque was destroyed."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would present now to Your Honours a copy of the next exhibit. It needs an exhibit number. It is a report on the devastation of cultural, historical, and natural heritage of the Republic Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina from April 5th, 1992, until September 5th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P972, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The document in front of you, Mr. Stavnjak, is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I could orient Your Honours to this document. First, this is a document -- if Your Honours turn to page 3 of the English, you will see a series at the top of abbreviations, and these abbreviations, A through O, describe the type of structure that will be described later in the tables that are attached. There is a number attached -- there is a number attached to edifice and it goes 1 through 4. You'll see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And that describes the amount of damage that relates to the document -- to the churches and mosques described in the -- later in the document. And if I direct your attention to page 8 of this document, there is another more refined subset of descriptions relating to the extent of damage, 1 to 5. And if I could direct Your Honours' attention to Cajnice, which is at page 30 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, according to this document, a number of mosques were damaged and destroyed in the municipality of Cajnice. First, we'll start with Cajnice, because there you said: "A few mosques had been destroyed." This list a number of mosques which are destroyed in that municipality. And are you able to read the list on page 30 of the mosques that are destroyed in Cajnice? Can you read English? If not ...

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This corresponds to my statement yesterday that in the territory of Gorazde, not a single mosque was destroyed, and a few mosques in the territory of Cajnice were destroyed. And this is precisely what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This shows in Cajnice, sir, that approximately nine mosques destroyed, and it shows that mehtebs, seven mehtebs, were completely burned down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon you're 15 minutes are up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I just have one more short --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll leave that and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to direct the witness's attention and Your Honours' attention to page 9 of the exhibit that's before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a list of mosques that are damaged and destroyed in the municipality of Gorazde. You'll see that there are 22 reference points in that list of mosques. If Your Honours go down to the next group, talking about imams, apartments, and mehtebs, you'll see that there are four of those types of buildings that are damaged and destroyed. And if Your Honours go down one more level, you'll see churches, that there is a parish church that is destroyed in Gorazde. So I submit this to Your Honours as evidence. And I'd like to put to the witness, Your Honour, the following question:

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, this compilation of survey of damage shows that approximately 22 mosques in the municipality of Cajnice were damaged or destroyed. Do you agree with that or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I really don't know. Cajnice is a very small municipality. I don't think I can agree that there is that many mosques. I'm not sure. I'm not sure about this fact. 22 mosques in Cajnice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to concentrate, Mr. Harmon, on what seems to be the real -- the category 4A appears five times, category 4 being the edifice was completely felled down, destroyed, no longer exists, and then A is destroyed by a deliberate fire. Witness, we see five times a category A. The first one is described as a mosque at Osjecani residential area, and the report says it was destroyed. Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I can't. I was nowhere near that place. I did not see any devastation. Not to this day I actually know what the devastation looks like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we then have to understand your testimony of yesterday limited to the town of Gorazde, where you said no mosque was destroyed? Was that about the town or the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The town itself. But I would like to say, if you allow me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll allow you to add something, but I then would like to ask you -- so you said about Osjecani, which also is under number 09, you wouldn't know about that. Old Oglecevi, do you know anything about a mosque being described there? Could you comment on the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you say "I have no knowledge of it" or do you say "the mosque is still there, so it must be wrong that it was described as being destroyed"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that information, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The same about Zigovi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no reason for me not to believe this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Would the same be true for destroyed mosque in Zigovi and Kopaci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that the testimony of the witness should be understood as limited to the town of Gorazde and not to cover at least -- at least the entries we just discussed on this list. Mr. Harmon, was this your last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Looking at the clock, apparently that will be my last question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No re-examination. Yes. Judge Hanoteau has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me come back to the incident which followed the explosion in a flat. You said that it was claimed, officially, that it was a gas cylinder which had exploded. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who claimed that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those were claims that I never had the opportunity to see in writing, but it came from MUP, from the police station. It was stated that Serbs in Gorazde used to say that the official statement, in fact, was that it was a gas cylinder which blew up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what makes you say that it wasn't a gas cylinder but, rather, a botched handling of an explosive device which was probably in the flat in question?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I heard from the neighbours of Serb nationality who lived in the immediate vicinity of the place where the incident happened, it wasn't a gas cylinder; they claimed that it was the actual explosives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, when this incident took place, there was no war. There were tensions between ethnic groups, but no armed conflict at the time.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no armed conflict, but later on, in the month of March, three or four months later, Serbs realised that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I would like us to stick to this point. This incident took place at a time when there was no armed conflict, at a time when there was no confusion or lack of organisation in terms of the institutions that existed in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If such an incident takes place in a municipality, say an explosion which destroys an apartment, presumably there would be an inquiry carried out by the police or the fire brigade or the municipal authorities. There must have been some official conclusions. Now I can see that you were a civil servant at the time; you worked at the municipality; you had certainly responsibilities, so you must have been up to date with the way in which inquiries were being carried out as to anything that took place in the municipality. So you would have had to find out about any reports which might have been drawn up following that incident.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to stress that the head of the police station at that particular time was a Muslim and he was a member of the SDA party, and he signed that report, or rather, the statement which was issued for the general public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. My question is: Did you ever see that official report?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How did you find out about it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Serbs in Gorazde discussed that incident because it was an incident which attracted the attention of both ethnic groups, and those were the comments that I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So those are comments that you heard, and they are making you call into question the official report; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's it. If you have a number of elements coming together pertaining to one and the same event, most Serbs, and I myself, were led to conclude that an explosive device was at the origin of the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. I have another question to do with the destruction of the Orthodox church, the church of St. George, as well as the adjoining apartment. You said it happened in September 1992; am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it happened at some point around the 1st of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. September, 1992, and I did see an official report which was drawn up by the police station of Serb Sarajevo in 1994. So the report was dated in 1994 and it gave a description of when the church was destroyed and the criminal report was filed against unknown perpetrators. And in that criminal report, there is also a reference to the fact that the adjoining residence in Gorazde was destroyed on the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you explain to us, very briefly, under what circumstances the church was destroyed, according to what you know about it.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know, because I was quite far away at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A third question: You talked about -- deftly of a procession of Muslim extremists from Visegrad led by a certain person, I didn't quite understand the name.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Mr. Murat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you be able to tell us what actually happened and why there was this procession of Muslim extremists, and where exactly did it take place?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Murat Sabanovic was cruising the centre of Gorazde, and I just drove by, but they were using megaphones. I didn't actually hear his exact words, but it was a bit out of the ordinary at the time. I mean, it was still a time of peace, and all the citizens of Gorazde used to live in town at the time, back then. And he grabbed the megaphone and acted almost as if there was no authority anywhere. That's what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it was when, exactly?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in April 1992. I wouldn't be able to tell you the exact date, but I think it was either mid-April, maybe the second half of April, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And who was this gentleman, Murat Sabatovic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a man from the municipality of Visegrad. That's where he resided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where did this procession take place exactly?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In town, along the streets, in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question now: You were asked by the Prosecution about the radio TV transmitter and the capture of that transmitter, and you said that you were not present but that you, yourself, saw it on TV. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to hear your reaction to that event. When you saw what was going on, how did you react? How did you place this incident within the overall context of this rather special atmosphere, which was very much in existence in your municipality at that time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean my own personal opinion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably it was because Serbs in Gorazde, as presumably most of the people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, disliked the rhetorical approach from TV Sarajevo, which was under the control of the representatives of the Muslim nationality, starting from the news broadcasts and everything else. So they were against it, and that's what I heard, and that's what the story was amongst Serbs in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, I do apologise. You referred to Serbs in general, but I was addressing you, in person. What was your personal view of the situation when you saw it? What was your personal reaction to that event? You were a citizen of that country. What was your reaction, in the face of that TV transmitter being taken over?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really have a reaction, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you think that it was completely illegal and unacceptable, or did you rather feel that, considering the atmosphere, the overall atmosphere at the time, it was something that could be considered acceptable?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a kind of atmosphere that nobody could keep under control. I've already mentioned this. It must have happened at some point in April, the second half of April. And it was extremely difficult to keep things under control. Already at that time, I can't remember whether at that time Mr. Murat Sabanvic used to come to Gorazde or not, but inter-ethnic tension was mounting and anything went, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anything was possible, both for Muslims and for Serbs?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Muslims as well. I mean, I don't have that information. But this transmitter was very close to the Serb villages and, presumably, that's the way it happened. There were Serb villages around, in the vicinity of the transmitter, I mean. And a little bit further afield, there were some Muslim villages, but Serbs probably got there first. That's the way things happened. There was no control at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me reiterate my question. It wasn't about finding out whether it was possible, but whether it was acceptable. Did you, yourself, feel that it was acceptable? Was just anything acceptable, any kind of behaviour on the part of both Serbs and Muslims at that particular time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my own personal point of view, no. Everything that went on at that time, as a human being, I must say that it was totally unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was what I was asking you about. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stavnjak, I would have a couple of questions for you as well. You told us that charges were brought in 1994 in relation to the destruction of the St. George Church. Do you remember that? Otherwise I'll try to find it.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened as a result of those charges? Was there someone convicted, sentenced?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all that is still in place. It was sent to the prosecution in Foca, and the actual documents were drafted by the police in 1994, the police station Serb Sarajevo. And this is a document that I actually saw. I had the opportunity to look at it and to read it through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't know what follow-up was given to that? I mean, I'd like to know whether someone was found guilty for it, whether someone was sentenced for it.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that kind of information. I really don't know what the follow-up was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to take you back to the television transmitter as well. Could you tell us where exactly it was located, perhaps on the basis of the map which is now part of the -- it now has become part of P954, but instead of having the whole of that document put before the witness -- that's the coloured ... Yes. Perhaps you'll put it on the ELMO, Madam Usher, so that we can ... Would you indicate where that television transmitter was located. If the other map would better serve you, we could look at the other map.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's right here, to the left of the village Borak Brdo, to the left here. It should be here. Just above Kanlici, Bogdanici and Borak Brdo, somewhere here, very close to this border, which is probably the border of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Close to the Rogatica municipality border. My next question is: Once this had happened, and I understand the incident to be that the Serbs took control over that television transmitter, did they keep it under their control, and if so, until when?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly until when, presumably until the 27th. I don't know until what time the Serbs had it under their control. I can't give you an exact date. But roughly speaking, probably up until the 27th of August, when Serbs basically left the area, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what television programmes could you receive before the takeover of the television transmitter, and what could you watch after it had been taken over by the Serbs? And perhaps I'm even more interested in what you could not see any more. You understand what I mean? What was the choice for those who were watching television before and after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that it was programmes of TV Belgrade were being broadcast, and you could no longer watch any programmes coming from TV Sarajevo. I think that was what was done. And there was some mechanics there, some technicians, it was there job. And there were some Serbs amongst them, and I think that they sorted things out in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So after the takeover, exclusively Belgrade, if I correctly understand. Now, what could you see, when you are talking about TV Sarajevo? Was that one programme? Was that a programme of any ethnic significance or signature, or how would I have to say that? Was it mixed? Was it Serb, Muslim, Croat, or were there more programmes? You understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understood you. In hindsight, as far as I can remember, I believe that we also had a so-called Yutel channel. This was the Yugoslav television, and it covered the entire area of the former Yugoslavia. That was the editorial policy at the time, and I believe that the programme's name or the channel's name was Yutel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that the only Sarajevo television channel? Is that the same as what you just said or is that a different channel?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the only television station that broadcast. It was Television Sarajevo, but at the time there was also another channel, Yutel. Sarajevo TV was the TV that provided us with all the programmes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what do you mean by "all the programmes"? Was this -- were these programmes exclusively addressing Muslims or Croats? I mean, were these programmes coloured by a certain ethnicity or did you have different programmes for all ethnicities? I'm trying to find out what was the variety of programmes you could receive before the takeover.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there were only these two channels, Sarajevo TV, and on the same channel you could also receive Yutel shows. And I believe that Yutel is an abbreviation standing for Yugoslav Television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that, but again, Sarajevo TV, the programmes they broadcast, were these programmes which were linked in anyway to exclusively one group of the population, or more groups? Did you have, well, say Croat programmes or Muslim programmes or Serb programmes from -- or was it just mono-ethnic, what they broadcast?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Serbian people in Gorazde at the time did not like the editorial policy of the news programmes of the then Sarajevo television station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. At the same time, were there other programmes, apart from the news?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time, everybody was involved in politics. They were eagerly awaiting to hear what happened here or there. This is what we all followed. And the focus of the media reporting was on the news, because the news at the time was the most popular show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there any debates on television among politicians, and would then politicians from different sides participate in that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question fully, but what I can say is this: When I spoke about the interest of people at the time in the news programmes, we remember the conversation amongst the six presidents of the six former republics of Yugoslavia. They went on a tour from one place to another. But when they ended their tour, we know what happened. Yugoslavia fell apart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to insist. If we are talking about shows, you could broadcast shows which were mainly Serb oriented or Muslim oriented or -- but the same for opinion programmes, that could be just mainly expressing the views of Serbs or of Croats or of Muslims. I'm trying to find out what exactly you could see before the takeover, apart from that you didn't like the way the news was presented.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the news reports on particular events that had been happening in some republics, such as Slovenia and Croatia, did not appeal to the population, and when the conflict spread on to Bosnia- Herzegovina, firstly, in the region called Posavina, then in Brod. Those reports, again, did not appeal to the Serbian people. They did not like the presentation of these reports as offered by the Television Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's not an answer to my question, because I excluded the news, but let's leave it to that for the time being. Did you have any knowledge of a Crisis Staff, a Serb Crisis Staff, established in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever learn about similar types of Serbian bodies which were specifically defending the Serb interests and political life, so well organised?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what they were?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you only about the things that I myself witnessed. Sometime in May, in Cajnice, a Crisis Staff was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but not such a thing as Serbian-organised organ, some kind of a Serbian organ that took place in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What about a Serbian War Presidency? Did that exist?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Gorazde? I don't know, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You read to us a letter yesterday which, as far as I understood, and I'm talking about Exhibit D90, that was a letter sent by the War Presidency of the Serbian Opstina of Gorazde. Would you have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I saw this document yesterday for the first time. I read it, but that was not the information that I had at the time about the municipality of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do I have to understand your testimony that this did not exist, such a War Presidency? Because you say that -- or would you say that at that time you didn't know about it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I really did not have that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the exhibits can be returned to the Registry. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. You told us that the police in Gorazde was split up; in what portions? Was it a Serb/non-Serb, or Croat/non-Croat, or Muslim/non- Muslim, or three portions?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this happened in the month of April. All Serb and Muslim policemen split. How, I wouldn't know. In any case, this happened in April. The Serb policemen went one way and the Muslim policemen went another way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they continue to work one next to the other, or how should I understand this?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that those who separated from the others started working independently. In any case, this was in the second half of April or in mid-April, or maybe in the second half of April or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday you told us that when you talked about Vitkovici, that it was under control of the Muslim forces. I did not fully understand. Was there a part of Gorazde municipality that was under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But how do I have to understand when you say Vitkovici was under control of the Muslim forces? So you're not certain about the whole of the municipality or --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vitkovici was under the control of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But does that make any sense to tell this, if not other parts of the municipality were under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It really depends on the period. It changed. The lines in Gorazde changed very often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And during which period did these lines change? I mean, when were the lines established for the first time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were established around the 4th or the 5th of May. The Serbian villages, the Serbian settlements existed, and likewise, the Muslim villages and settlements that they controlled for their safety. On the 18th and 19th September, the line moved radically, when we're talking about the right bank. As for the left bank of the Drina, this happened on the 27th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You told us about who were with you when you tried to cross the river three times with your car, one of them being Mr. Krunic. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Marko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You were stopped by the police, and Mr. Krunic had a weapon. Was this weapon taken from him or could he keep it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could keep it. He was an active policeman. He was a police officer, and he had an official pistol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And was that before the police was divided or was it after?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR STAVNJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say which event preceded the other, but this all happened within the space of a couple of days. The police still worked together. If they had not worked together, I believe that the pistol would have been taken away from Mr. Krunic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That sounds a bit like speculation, but I can imagine that you had that expectation. These were my questions to you. Did the questions of the Bench raise any need for further questions by the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These were my questions. Since we have no further questions for you, I would like to thank you very much, Mr. Stavnjak, for having come to The Hague and having answered the questions of the parties and of the Bench. I hope you have a safe trip home again, and you are excused. Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would now like to deal with the exhibits, but we have several problems as far as translation is concerned. Fortunately, not only Defence problems, but I also saw some Prosecution exhibits in English only, without B/C/S translation, Mr. Harmon, especially the Tanjug report and other documents are not available in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We listened to the evidence of this witness and we were able to collect those without having time to have them translated. We will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's what happens now and then, so all parties know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's start. It was a Defence witness -- Defence Exhibit D89, which is a map marked by the witness; any objection, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it's admitted into evidence. Then we have D90. Mr. Stewart, we are still waiting for an English translation of that document, which is the letter answer to the Muslim people and Muslim Assembly of the Gorazde municipality. The Chamber would like to have a written translation and not just work on the basis of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yell, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there was a second document, although I think it was not -- it was on your list, but then not put to the witness, if I am correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It was put to the witness. It was very brief, Your Honour, because he -- I think he said he had never seen it before and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you tender that into evidence? Because if the witness has not seen the document, it might not make --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's not necessary at this point, Your Honour, if - -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no. It was the document that was already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If it was already in, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise for the mistake I made. That means that D90 is still pending and D89 is admitted into evidence. We now turn to the exhibits tendered by the Prosecution, starting with P965. That is the -- it says the map of Gorazde municipality, but I think, as a matter of fact, it is the census figures, no? That's --no. Map of Gorazde municipality. Let me just have a look at it. Yes. I will show it to you, Mr. Stewart, any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, not from this distance, or at all, I think, Your Honour. No, there's no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As usual, we find them in the other binder. Then 965 is admitted into evidence. We have P966, the letter sent to President Karadzic, dated the 25th of May. And I'll -- yes, perhaps I'll do that first. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's, then, admitted into evidence. Then we have the handwritten notes on the P967. There is an English translation. Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the ones, Your Honour, where we'd quite like some sorting out as to what exactly they are said to be. But Mr. Harmon has helpfully indicated that he will pursue that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's our submission, Your Honour, that these are notes that were retrieved in Gorazde. These reflect Variant A and Variant B, these handwritten notes, and they reflect the implementation of those -- at least elements from Variant A and Variant B in the municipality of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's a submission as to what they do, Your Honour, not as to what they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I've said what they are, and they are notes that were recovered in Gorazde, provided to us by the Bosnian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but do we have any further details as where exactly? Because when I asked you, you said where another document was found and not this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, there are two documents, Your Honour. There's Variant A and Variant B. I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand that you explained where that was found. Now, is it known where this was found?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will make a further inquiry, Your Honour, and find out exactly. I know it was found in the Gorazde -- retrieved in the Gorazde municipality by the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, of course, it could make quite some difference whether it's found in a home inhabited by a Serb or in the party offices of either SDA or SDS. That might make a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I intend to make a further inquiry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we have that part of the document, which you presented as one document, which relates to October. Is that something you would still want to make --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will present a contextual document in respect of that to show what happened in October, that it's our submission gave rise to this particular October portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then the reason why these documents at this moment are together is on the basis of that present presumption that they were found together?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'll further hear from you about the October roster.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I take it that we are not deciding on admission at this moment. And for Mr. Registrar, there is a translation, P967.1. I'll write that down. Then media report, Tanjug, P968. There's no B/C/S translation yet. And we would learn about -- or you would explain to us, Mr. Harmon, why we find on the top of this document and also on, I think was that P969, why we find the black boxes at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will be glad to, Your Honour. May I go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. So P968 and P969 are now awaiting for translation before a decision of admission will be taken. P970 has not yet -- there's no B/C/S translation yet, Mr. Harmon. B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Not yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait for that. The P971 I think is the same, no translation yet. It is a relatively short document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait for a translation before any decision will be taken on admission. And then, finally, P972, the report of the Institute for Protection of Cultural and Natural Heritage of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, where there is -- that's also in English only. I wonder, Mr. Stewart -- I don't know whether there is a B/C/S translation, whether that exists, Mr. Harmon. If not, I wonder whether we should engage into translations of many, many pages just listing mosques in the various municipalities, or whether, for example, we could limit ourselves to perhaps the first seven pages and then only the relevant portions. Because this is a document of which I think it would really make not much sense to have this all translated at this moment, although the Rule is there. The Chamber wants to be very strict on the matter. I really ask myself whether, with the consent of the parties, we could not find a practical solution for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, with respect, what Your Honour says makes a great deal of sense. We're not particularly interested either way with translations where the content is really pretty obvious without that. So we certainly, with respect, endorse Your Honour's approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would suggest the following: No decision is taken at this moment about admission into evidence. We expect the Defence to come up, within the next ten days, with a position as far as whether, at all, a translation would be needed, and if so, whether it could be limited to certain portions of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's all, as far as the exhibits are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was one exhibit, Your Honour, that I mentioned, about Vitkovici, contextual document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have that document. If I could present that, at least have it marked as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that that would be the only contextual exhibit on Gorazde, or --?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because we usually waited until the end of the testimony on a certain municipality and then have at one occasion the contextual exhibits not presented to a witness tendered, and then we would hear from the Defence whether there would be any objections, or whether the Chamber would have any hesitations. So if it's the last one, then I have no problem. If it's not, then I'd rather would invite you to wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm at your disposal, Your Honours. I don't know if this is the last witness for Gorazde, because I'm not calling these witnesses. Mr. Stewart is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the same thought, of course, is occurring to me, that Mr. Harmon can't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're not inclined, but really, in the Trial Chamber's hands here, whatever is more convenient. Because certainly, the Defence is not going to insist that we wait until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- the last Gorazde witness should come along. It doesn't really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've looked at these documents. Have you made up your mind as to whether there's any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, there's no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Then if a copy could be given to -- a number should be assigned. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P973, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look on whether it's available in both languages. It's only in English. Mr. Harmon, therefore, this contextual document, we will decide once a B/C/S translation has been provided, and it's already on the record that there's no objection from the Defence. Then is there anything else? Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was a question put to the witness by me in respect of Vojislav Krunic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And whether he was a member of the SDS Executive Board in 1991 and 1992. That information is found in Mr. Treanor's report, I'm informed, at annexes 7 and 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It seems a lot of people had the name of Krunic in that municipality. I think we came across three of them already. Thank you for that information. Is there anything else, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon. We'll then adjourn until tomorrow, at a quarter past 2.00, in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
